title: Foundations and Performance
subtitle: Speed, size, uptime and growth: the vocabulary of every design

scenes.title: Foundations and Performance
scenes.subtitle: Speed, size, uptime and growth: the vocabulary of every design

steps.say: Welcome to episode one of the System Design Workshop. By the end you'll be able to size a system with real numbers, explain latency, percentiles and the nines, scale a service out, and run a design interview step by step.
We'll follow one running example most of the way: a photo-sharing app, like an early Instagram. Every time a slide lists steps or types, we'll apply each one to that app, with numbers.
Keep the Part one notes open: each concept matches a section there, in order. Pause on any calculation and redo it yourself.

scenes.title: What system design is
bullets: Parts, jobs, connections, where data lives
Coding: one program. Design: many machines
Scale breaks the shape, not the loops
Two working designs can differ 10x in cost

steps.say: System design is deciding which parts software needs, what each does, how they talk, and where the data lives, so the whole meets its goals for users, speed, uptime and cost.
Coding asks how one function works. Design asks how twenty programs on two hundred machines cooperate without losing data. Like an architect: floors and fire exits, not bricks.

A program that works for ten users can collapse at ten million because its shape is wrong. One database everyone queues for, one machine whose death kills the site. Better loops don't fix that. Design does.
And two working designs can differ ten times over in their cloud bill.

scenes.title: The design loop
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["1. Understand the goal"] --> B["2. Estimate the load"]
  B --> C["3. Sketch the parts"]
  C --> D["4. Find weak spots"]
  D --> E["5. Fix and justify"]
  E --> A
scenes.caption: A design is right for a given load, never finished

steps.say: Design runs as a loop of five steps. Understand the goal. Estimate the load. Sketch the parts. Find the weak spots. Fix it and justify the fix. Then go round again as the system grows.
That's easy to say and hard to picture, so let's run the loop once, step by step, on our photo app.

scenes.title: The design loop, run once on a photo app

head: Step
Applied to the photo app
rows: Upload, feed; p99 under 200 ms; 99.9% up
LB, app servers, 1 database, object storage
DB swamped at peak; DB is the single failure
Cache (250:1 reads) + standby DB; cost named

steps.say: Step one, understand the goal: what it must do, and how well. Our app lets people upload photos and scroll a feed. How well: the feed loads in under two hundred milliseconds for ninety-nine percent of requests, and the app is up ninety-nine point nine percent of the time.

Step two, estimate the load. Ten million people a day each view fifty photos: about five thousand reads a second on average, fifteen thousand at the evening peak. We'll do this maths properly in concept nine.
Step three, sketch the parts. Phones talk to a load balancer, which spreads requests over a few app servers. They store photo details in one database and the image files in object storage.

Step four, find the weak spots. What runs out first? One database handles roughly one to ten thousand simple queries a second, so fifteen thousand reads at peak will swamp it. What takes everything down? That same database. If it dies, the app dies.

Step five, fix and justify. Add a cache in front of the database, because there are two hundred and fifty reads for every write. Add a standby database in another building. Then say the cost: the cache can show slightly stale data, and the standby costs money.
Then the loop restarts. At ten times the users, step four finds a new weak spot, maybe the cache or the network. A design is right for a given load, never finished.

scenes.title: Abstractions leak, choices cost
bullets: Abstraction: a simple contract over details
Leaks: a cache still showing a deleted photo
Every choice is a trade-off: name it

steps.say: Your main tool is abstraction: a simple contract hiding the details. A remote call that looks like a local function. A database that looks like one table but is really many machines.
Abstractions leak. Networks fail halfway, replicas lag, clocks drift. Our new cache is one: delete a photo, and the cache may show it for another minute.
Every choice gives something up. More copies are safer but cost more and can disagree. Say the trade-off out loud.
In the interview there's rarely one right answer. They grade the reasoning: questions, estimates, chosen parts, and trade-offs.

scenes.title: Clients, servers and request/response
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  B["Browser"] -->|"1. DNS lookup"| N["DNS"]
  B -->|"2. GET /profile"| S["Server"]
  S -->|"3. look up user 42"| D["Database"]
  D -->|"4. name, photo, bio"| S
  S -->|"5. 200 OK + HTML"| B
scenes.caption: A client asks, a server answers

steps.say: A client is any program that asks: a browser, an app, or another server. A server waits for requests and answers them. On the web they speak H-T-T-P, a standard request and response format. Let's follow one request through the five numbered arrows.
Arrow one. You open example dot com slash profile. The browser doesn't know where example dot com lives, so it asks D-N-S, the internet's phone book, and gets back an address.
Arrow two. The browser connects to that address and sends a request: GET slash profile.
Arrow three. The server reads it, sees you're user forty-two, and asks the database for your record.
Arrow four. The database replies with your name, photo and bio.

Arrow five. The server replies two hundred, O-K, with the page, and the browser draws it. Notice that in arrow three the server was itself a client. Inside big systems, servers are clients of other servers all the time.

scenes.title: Variations to know
bullets: Thin client: web page. Thick: mobile game
Pull by default; push for chat
A server is a role, not one box
The network is slow and unreliable

steps.say: A thin client relies on the server: a basic web page that fetches everything. A thick client does a lot locally: a mobile game that only calls home to save your score.
Normally the client pulls. A chat app needs the server to push a new message to you unasked, using WebSockets or server-sent events. That's episode two.
A server is a role, not a box. One name, like api dot example dot com, is often hundreds of machines behind a load balancer.
And the network between them is slow and unreliable compared with work inside one machine. Recap: almost everything on the web is a chain of request and response, often server to server.

scenes.title: The building blocks of a web app

head: Part
Job in the photo app
rows: Rules: who may see a photo; copies

steps.say: Nearly every web app uses the same eight parts. Here's each one's job in our photo app. The client renders the interface: the phone app showing your feed.
The load balancer spreads requests over app servers and skips dead ones. Fifteen thousand feed requests a second get shared across the fleet.
App servers apply business rules, like only followers may see a private photo. You run identical copies so one crash doesn't stop the site.
The database stores data durably: who posted which photo, captions, likes. It's usually the hardest part to scale, because it holds state.
A cache keeps hot data in RAM. Today's popular feed comes back in well under a millisecond, versus several milliseconds or more from the database.
A queue plus workers runs slow jobs later. Making three thumbnail sizes of an upload goes on the queue, so the upload returns at once.
Object storage holds big files by key, like photos slash forty-two slash beach. Databases are bad at large files.
A C-D-N, content delivery network, keeps copies of the images near users, so someone in Sydney doesn't fetch every photo from Virginia.

scenes.title: How the boxes connect
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U["Users"] --> CDN["CDN"]
  U --> LB["Load balancer"]
  LB --> A["App servers"]
  A --> C["Cache"]
  A --> DB["Database"]
  A --> Q["Queue + workers"]
  Q --> OS["Object storage"]
scenes.caption: Justify every box with a problem or a number

steps.say: Now trace one upload. The phone sends the photo through the load balancer to an app server. The server saves the caption in the database, stores the file in object storage, and drops a make-thumbnails job on the queue. It replies at once. A worker picks up the job later and writes the thumbnails to object storage.

Now trace one feed view. The app server asks the cache first. On a hit, done in under a millisecond. On a miss, it reads the database and fills the cache. The images themselves come from the C-D-N, not your servers.
Instagram's early stack looked almost exactly like this. Add a box only when you can name its problem. A small internal tool may need just one server and one database.

scenes.title: Building-block mistakes
bullets: Files in object storage, keys in the database
Slow work goes on a queue
One server: a SPOF with a hard limit
Queues for slow, deferrable, bursty work

steps.say: Don't store images in the database. Put files in object storage and keep only the key.
Don't do slow work, like video encoding, inside the web request. Queue it.
Interview question: why not one server? It's a single point of failure with a hard capacity limit. Stateless app servers behind a load balancer let you add machines and survive crashes.
And add a queue when work is slow, can wait, or arrives in bursts. Recap: each box solves one problem.
Three kinds of speed. Latency is how long one request takes, in milliseconds or microseconds.
Throughput is how many requests finish per second.
Bandwidth is the most a link can carry per second, in bits. The width of the pipe.
On a motorway, latency is one car's journey time, throughput is cars actually arriving per hour, and bandwidth is the number of lanes.
Strictly, response time is what the client feels: network both ways, plus queueing, plus service time. In interviews latency usually means response time.

Latency and bandwidth are independent. A satellite link has huge bandwidth and six hundred millisecond round trips. More bandwidth won't speed up a small A-P-I call. And throughput sets fleet size: fifty thousand requests a second at a thousand per server needs at least fifty servers.

scenes.title: Where latency comes from
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Propagation: ~200 km per ms"] --> B["Transmission: size / bandwidth"]
  B --> C["Queueing: waiting in line"]
  C --> D["Processing: the real work"]
scenes.caption: Near 100% utilisation, queues grow and latency explodes

steps.say: Every request picks up four kinds of delay. Propagation: the time for the signal to travel. Transmission: the time to push the bytes onto the wire. Queueing: waiting behind other requests. Processing: the real work.

Load links them. At low load latency is flat. Near full use, requests wait for each other and latency explodes while throughput levels off. That's why teams run at fifty to seventy percent at peak. Let's put real numbers on all four.

scenes.title: One photo page, London to New York

head: Delay
Calculation
Time
rows: 5,600 km / 200 km per ms, both ways

steps.say: Imagine a user in London opening a photo page served from New York. The page carries a one megabyte photo, and the user is on a hundred megabit connection.

Propagation. Light in fibre covers about two hundred kilometres per millisecond. London to New York is fifty-six hundred kilometres, so at least twenty-eight milliseconds one way. Real cables wiggle and routers add delay, so a round trip is about seventy.
Transmission. One megabyte is eight megabits. At a hundred megabits a second that takes eighty milliseconds. At one gigabit, just eight. This is the only term bandwidth helps.
Queueing. Say the server is ninety percent busy at peak. Our request waits behind others, say thirty milliseconds.
Processing. The database query and building the page, say fifteen milliseconds.

Total: about a hundred and ninety-five milliseconds. Each delay has its own fix. A C-D-N copy in London cuts seventy to about ten. Compressing the photo to two hundred kilobytes cuts eighty to sixteen. Headroom shrinks the queue. An index speeds the query.

scenes.title: The low-latency checklist
bullets: 5 sequential calls x 70 ms = 350 ms; batch: 70
Move bytes closer; cache; defer work
Smaller payloads, indexes, headroom, cut tail
Name the price of every lever
Pause: Australia to Virginia. More bandwidth?

steps.say: Start with a latency budget. For a p ninety-nine target of two hundred milliseconds on the feed, give sixty to the network, twenty to the gateway, eighty to the service and database, forty as slack. Whoever overspends gets fixed first.

Remove round trips. Say the feed screen makes five calls one after another from London to Virginia, at seventy milliseconds each: three hundred and fifty milliseconds. Batch them into one call and it's seventy. Reuse connections so you don't repeat handshakes.
Move bytes closer with C-D-Ns. Serve hot reads from memory. Defer work like thumbnails onto the queue.
Then shrink payloads, index queries, keep headroom, and cut the tail with deadlines and hedged requests. Measure every hop.
Name each lever's price: caches go stale, replicas cost money, async work shows results later.
Pause and think: a user in Australia is slow against servers in Virginia. Will more bandwidth help?
Barely. The round trip is about two hundred milliseconds. Cut round trips: a nearby C-D-N, fewer sequential calls, reused connections, maybe a regional deployment.
Don't mix bits and bytes. A hundred megabits per second moves at most twelve and a half megabytes per second.
Batching raises throughput but adds latency: the first write waits for the other ninety-nine.
Recap: a cargo ship has high throughput and high latency. A motorbike courier is the reverse.

A percentile is the value below which that percentage of measurements fall. A p ninety-five of three hundred milliseconds means ninety-five percent finished within three hundred. p fifty is the median.
p ninety: one request in ten is slower.
p ninety-five: one in twenty.
p ninety-nine: one in a hundred.
p ninety-nine point nine: one in a thousand. This slow end of the graph is called tail latency.
Here's a real-looking request log. Ten feed requests: nine take ten milliseconds, and one hits a garbage-collection pause and takes a thousand. To read percentiles, sort them and count positions.
The mean adds them up, one thousand and ninety, and divides by ten: a hundred and nine milliseconds. No request took a hundred and nine. The average describes nobody.
p fifty, the median, sits in the middle, the fifth and sixth values: ten milliseconds. The typical user is happy.
p ninety is the ninth value out of ten: still ten milliseconds.
p ninety-five lands past the ninth value, on the tenth: a thousand milliseconds.

p ninety-nine is the tenth value too: a full second. So one user in ten waited a second, and only the high percentiles show it. Real latency is skewed like this, by pauses, cache misses and retries. Percentiles show the shape. Averages flatten it.

scenes.title: Fan-out amplifies the tail
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U["User request"] --> F["Front end waits for ALL"]
  F --> S1["Server 1 fast"]
  F --> S2["Server 2 fast"]
  F --> S3["Server 3 slow 1% of time"]
  F --> SN["... Server 100"]
  S3 --> R["User sees slowest reply"]
scenes.caption: 1 - 0.99^100 = about 63% of user requests hit a slow server

steps.say: The tail matters more than it looks. A heavy user who loads a hundred pages a day hits your p ninety-nine about once a day. And heavy users are often your best customers.
Worse is fan-out. Imagine photo search: one user request asks a hundred search servers in parallel and waits for all of them. Each server is slow just one percent of the time.

The chance all hundred are fast is point nine nine to the power of a hundred, about thirty-seven percent. So about sixty-three percent of searches hit a slow server. One in a hundred per server becomes two in three for the user. That's from Google's paper, The Tail at Scale.

scenes.title: Measuring and cutting the tail
bullets: Hedge after p95 (50 ms): ~5% extra requests

steps.say: Monitoring uses histograms, counts per latency bucket, to estimate percentiles without storing every value.
Never average percentiles across servers. Merge the histograms instead.

Cut the tail with hedged requests. Say the search server's p ninety-five is fifty milliseconds. If no reply after fifty, ask a second replica and take whichever answers first. That costs only about five percent extra requests, and rescues the slow ones. Add timeouts and limit fan-out.
Beware coordinated omission: a load tester that waits on each slow response sends less traffic exactly then, hiding the tail.

Interview question: your service's p ninety-nine is fine but users still complain. Why? Each page calls many services, so the chance of at least one slow call per page is far above one percent. Look at end-to-end latency. Recap: percentiles, not averages.

scenes.title: Little's law
scenes.caption: In flight = arrival rate x time in system

steps.say: Little's law holds for any stable system, where items arrive, spend some time, and leave. L equals lambda times W.

L is the number of items inside at once, like requests in flight. Lambda is the arrival rate, which in a stable system equals throughput. W is the time each item spends inside: the latency. Know any two and you get the third.

scenes.title: Little's law in a coffee shop

steps.say: Picture a coffee shop. Let's find each of the three letters.
Lambda, the arrival rate: two customers walk in every minute.
W, the time inside: each customer queues, gets a drink and sits for ten minutes.
So L, the number inside on average, is two times ten: twenty people. That's true whatever the barista does. It's just counting.
Now the barista slows down and each visit stretches to fifteen minutes. Same arrivals, so thirty people inside. With twenty seats, ten are standing. Slower service means more people in the building.
Run it backwards. The shop has twenty seats and visits last ten minutes, so it can serve at most twenty divided by ten: two customers a minute. That's the same sum we'll do for servers.

Now swap customers for requests. Our feed service gets a thousand requests a second, and each takes point two seconds. A thousand times point two is two hundred in flight. So you need at least two hundred threads or connections, plus headroom, or requests queue.

Run it backwards for a database pool. Twenty connections, each query takes five milliseconds, which is point zero zero five seconds. Twenty divided by point zero zero five: at most four thousand queries a second.
And here's why slow dependencies hurt. Keep the twenty connections, but the database slows to ten milliseconds a query. Max throughput halves, to two thousand. Same hardware, half the capacity.
Two rules: the system must be stable, and convert milliseconds to seconds first. Pause: a hundred threads, each held two hundred and fifty milliseconds. Max throughput?
A hundred divided by point two five: four hundred requests a second. Beyond that, requests queue and latency climbs.

scenes.title: Latency numbers every engineer should know

head: Operation
Approx. time
rows: Round trip in one data centre

steps.say: From Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig. Learn orders of magnitude, not digits. An L one cache read, inside the processor: one nanosecond.
A RAM read: a hundred nanoseconds.
A random four kilobyte read from a fast N-V-M-e S-S-D: twenty to a hundred microseconds.
A round trip inside one data centre: half a millisecond.
One megabyte read sequentially from S-S-D: point two to one millisecond.
A hard disk seek: ten milliseconds, because an arm physically moves.
London to New York round trip: seventy milliseconds.
California to Europe: a hundred and fifty.

scenes.title: If one nanosecond were one second
scenes.big: L1 1 s, RAM 2 min, DC trip 6 days, HDD seek 4 months, ocean 2 years
scenes.caption: Orders of magnitude matter, not exact digits

steps.say: Scale it up to human time. If an L one read took a second, a RAM read would take about two minutes, a data-centre round trip about six days, a disk seek four months, and London to New York two years.

scenes.title: Pricing one feed request with the table

steps.say: Let's use the table to price parts of one feed request in our photo app.

The feed needs twenty pieces of data from Redis. Fetched one after another, each costs a data-centre round trip of half a millisecond: ten milliseconds. The RAM read inside Redis is nanoseconds. The trip is what you pay for.
Batch them into one multi-get call and it's one round trip: half a millisecond. Twenty times faster, same data.
Now a cache miss sends ten random reads to a database. On S-S-D, at about a hundred microseconds each, that's about one millisecond.
If that database sat on spinning disks, ten seeks at ten milliseconds is a hundred milliseconds. Half our whole budget gone on disk arms. That's why databases moved to S-S-Ds.

And a call to another continent adds seventy to a hundred and fifty milliseconds. Only moving data closer fixes that. Interview version: fifty sequential calls of a millisecond is fifty milliseconds before any real work. Batch or parallelise.

scenes.title: What the numbers tell you
bullets: RAM >> SSD >> HDD: caches live in RAM
Oceans cost 70-150 ms: move data closer

steps.say: RAM is a hundred to a thousand times faster than S-S-D for random reads, so caches live in RAM.
A data-centre round trip costs as much as thousands of memory reads. A thousand sequential database calls cost at least half a second in trips alone.
Ocean crossings cost seventy to a hundred and fifty milliseconds, and light isn't getting faster.
Sequential beats random, so storage engines write append-only logs. Recap: memory is nanoseconds, S-S-D microseconds, network and disk milliseconds.

head: Unit
Bytes
Roughly holds
rows: A photo, a minute of MP3
Part of an hour of HD video
A laptop drive; a day of photos

steps.say: A byte is eight bits, enough for one letter. Each unit is about a thousand times the last. Two to the ten is ten twenty-four, but estimates round it to a thousand. A kilobyte: a short post with its metadata.
A megabyte: a high-quality photo, or a minute of M-P-three.
A gigabyte: an hour of streamed H-D video is a few of these.
A terabyte: a laptop drive. Our photo app takes in one of these every day.
A petabyte: a large company's data warehouse. Our app reaches nearly two of these in five years.

scenes.title: Numbers to keep in your pocket
bullets: Timestamp 8 B, UUID 16 B, photo 0.2-2 MB

steps.say: Two to the thirty-two is about four point three billion. That's every I-P version four address, and where a thirty-two bit I-D column runs out. A signed one runs out at about two billion rows.
A timestamp is eight bytes, a U-U-I-D sixteen. A compressed photo is two hundred kilobytes to two megabytes. A minute of H-D video, twenty-five to sixty megabytes.
A day is eighty-six thousand four hundred seconds. Round it to ten to the five, a hundred thousand.
So one million per day is about twelve per second. For example, a shop taking three million orders a day handles about thirty-six a second on average.
And a one gigabit network card moves a hundred and twenty-five megabytes per second at best, because there are eight bits in a byte.

scenes.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Assumptions: DAU, actions, size"] --> B["Requests per day"]
  B --> C["Average QPS = per day / 100,000"]
  C --> D["Peak QPS = average x 2 to 3"]
  B --> E["Storage per day = items x size"]
  E --> F["Total = per day x days x replicas"]
  C --> G["Bandwidth = QPS x size"]
scenes.caption: Round aggressively, state every assumption

steps.say: A back-of-the-envelope estimate finds the order of magnitude, and that decides the architecture. A hundred requests a second fits one server. A hundred thousand needs caching and sharding.
Start from assumptions. D-A-U means daily active users. Multiply by actions per user to get requests per day.
Divide by ten to the five to get average Q-P-S, queries per second.
Multiply by two or three for the peak, because traffic bunches up in the evening. More for spiky products like ticket sales.

Storage per day is new items times their size. Total storage is that times days kept, times replicas. And bandwidth is Q-P-S times response size. Say every assumption out loud. Now the photo app, one line at a time.

Assumptions, said out loud: ten million daily users, each viewing fifty photos and uploading point two a day. Photos average five hundred kilobytes, metadata one kilobyte, and we keep everything five years.
Reads. Ten million times fifty is five hundred million views a day. Divide by ten to the five: about five thousand Q-P-S average, fifteen thousand at a three times peak.
Writes. Ten million times point two is two million uploads a day: about twenty per second, sixty at peak. That's two hundred and fifty reads per write, so caching and a C-D-N matter a lot.
Storage per day. Two million times five hundred kilobytes is one terabyte of photos a day, plus two gigabytes of metadata.

Five years. One terabyte times three sixty-five times five is about one point eight petabytes, times three with replicas. Photos go in object storage. Metadata, about three point six terabytes, fits a sharded database.
Bandwidth. Five thousand views a second times five hundred kilobytes is two and a half gigabytes per second, about twenty gigabits. A strong case for a C-D-N.

scenes.title: How many servers do we need?

steps.say: Now server count, the step interviewers love. Assume thirty thousand requests a second at peak. Each uses four milliseconds of C-P-U and takes fifty milliseconds end to end. Sixteen-core machines, three availability zones, and we must survive losing one. Step one: one core does a thousand divided by four, two hundred and fifty per second.
Step two: times sixteen cores, four thousand per server at full load.
Step three: keep C-P-U at sixty percent so queues stay short. Twenty-four hundred per server.
Step four: thirty thousand divided by twenty-four hundred is twelve and a half. Round up to thirteen.
Step five, a Little's law check: thirty thousand times point zero five is fifteen hundred in flight, about a hundred and fifteen per server. Fine.
Step six, zone loss: thirteen must survive with two zones left, so seven per zone. Times three zones: twenty-one.
Step seven: rolling deploys take about ten percent out at a time, so roughly twenty-three servers.
Step eight, network: twenty kilobyte responses give about four point eight gigabits total, about a quarter gigabit per server. C-P-U is the limit, not the network.

scenes.title: Reading the answer
bullets: CPU per request sets the fleet

steps.say: The naive answer, thirty thousand over four thousand, was eight. The ceiling and zone-loss rule explain the gap of about three times.
C-P-U per request set the number. Halve it and you halve the fleet.
Repeat per tier: caches are limited by memory, databases by disk and writes.
Common mistakes: forgetting peak, replicas and index overhead, and false precision. Spend three to five minutes, out loud.
Pause: a hundred million daily users, twenty requests each. Plan for what Q-P-S?
Two billion a day over ten to the five is twenty thousand average, about sixty thousand at peak. For scale, WhatsApp's hundred billion messages a day is about a million per second.

Availability is the share of time a system works correctly: uptime over total time, or successful requests over valid ones. Two nines, ninety-nine percent, allows three point six five days down a year, seven point two hours a month.
Three nines, ninety-nine point nine: eight point seven six hours a year, forty-three minutes a month, about a minute and a half a day.
Ninety-nine point nine five: four point three eight hours a year, about twenty-two minutes a month.
Four nines: fifty-three minutes a year, four point three minutes a month. Less than a human needs to wake up and log in, so recovery must be automatic.
Five nines: about five minutes a year. Each nine cuts downtime ten times, and usually costs far more than ten times the effort.

scenes.title: A real outage against the nines

steps.say: Let's measure a real outage with this table. In February twenty seventeen, Amazon S-three in its biggest U-S region went down for about four hours.
The cause was human. An engineer ran a routine command to remove a few servers, mistyped one input, and removed far more than intended. Thousands of websites that stored files there broke with it.
Against a three nines yearly budget of eight point seven six hours, that one afternoon used about half the year.
Against a monthly target of ninety-nine point nine, which allows forty-three minutes, four hours drops that month to about ninety-nine point four percent.
Against four nines, fifty-three minutes a year, the budget was blown more than four times over. One bad afternoon decides your nines.

scenes.title: Series and parallel
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Series["Series: all must work = 99.79%"]
    A1["LB 99.99%"] --> A2["App 99.9%"] --> A3["DB 99.9%"]
  end
  subgraph Parallel["Parallel: one is enough = 99.99%"]
    B1["Server A 99%"]
    B2["Server B 99%"]
  end
scenes.caption: Series multiplies down. Redundancy multiplies up

steps.say: Now, how parts combine. Parts in series must all work, so you multiply. A feed request goes through a load balancer at four nines, an app tier at three, and a database at three. Point nine nine nine nine times point nine nine nine times point nine nine nine: about ninety-nine point seven nine percent. Lower than the weakest link.

Parts in parallel need only one to work. Two independent servers at ninety-nine percent are both down only one percent of one percent of the time: ninety-nine point nine nine. Two cheap two-nines machines make a four-nines pair.
But only if failures are independent. Put both in one rack, and one power cut takes both.

scenes.title: Costs and traps
bullets: 3 to 4 nines: often double the infra
Recap: 43 min vs 4.3 min a month

steps.say: Going from three nines to four can mean several data centres and double the infrastructure. Many internal tools are fine at ninety-nine point five.
Cloud S-L-As for single services are usually three or four nines. S-three is designed for four nines but its contract promises three.
Planned maintenance still counts as downtime. Users don't care why it's down.

Interview question: how do you beat any single machine's availability? Redundant copies in parallel across racks, zones or regions, with automatic failover and no single points of failure. Recap: three nines is forty-three minutes a month, four nines about four.

scenes.title: SLI, SLO and SLA
bullets: Pizza: actual times, 95% in 30 min, free at 45

steps.say: Three terms, from most technical to most legal. An S-L-I, service level indicator, is a measurement.
An S-L-O, service level objective, is an internal target for that measurement.
An S-L-A, service level agreement, is a contract with customers, with penalties, usually service credits.

Think of a pizza shop. The S-L-I is how long deliveries actually take. The S-L-O is the manager's ninety-five percent within thirty minutes. The S-L-A is the printed promise: over forty-five minutes and it's free. The S-L-A is looser, so missing the S-L-O warns you before you have to pay.

scenes.title: SLI, SLO and SLA for the photo feed

steps.say: Now one real service: our photo app's feed A-P-I, serving a hundred million requests a month.
The S-L-I: the percentage of feed requests that succeed in under three hundred milliseconds, measured over thirty days.
The S-L-O: ninety-nine point nine percent of them.
The S-L-A: ninety-nine point five percent, or business customers get ten percent of their bill back. Looser on purpose.
The error budget is one minus the S-L-O: point one percent. Of a hundred million requests, a hundred thousand may fail this month.

Incident one. A bad deploy fails two percent of requests for an hour. An hour is about a hundred and thirty-nine thousand requests, so about twenty-eight hundred failed. That's under three percent of the budget. Roll back and keep shipping.

Incident two. The database dies and the feed is down for thirty minutes: about seventy thousand failures, seventy percent of the budget. The team freezes risky launches and works on failover. Still inside the S-L-A, so no refunds. The warning came first.

scenes.title: Error budgets
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  I["SLI measured: 99.95%"] --> O["SLO target: 99.9%"]
  O --> B["Error budget left"]
  B -->|"budget left"| F["Keep shipping features"]
  B -->|"budget spent"| R["Freeze risky changes"]
  O --> A["SLA looser, e.g. 99.5%: refunds"]
scenes.caption: Error budget = 1 - SLO

steps.say: So the budget turns reliability into a shared decision. While budget remains, ship fast. When it's spent, freeze risky changes and fix reliability. The idea comes from Google's site reliability engineering.

Rules of thumb: pick indicators users feel, like failed checkouts, not C-P-U. Never set an S-L-O of a hundred percent, because any change would violate it. Measure over a rolling thirty days, and alert when the budget burns too fast.

Two measures of failure. M-T-B-F, mean time between failures, is how long a system runs before it breaks. Higher is better. M-T-T-R, mean time to repair or recover, is how long it stays broken. Lower is better.
Availability is M-T-B-F divided by M-T-B-F plus M-T-T-R. There's also M-T-T-D, mean time to detect: how long before anyone notices. Detection is part of repair.

scenes.title: One database, two ways to recover

steps.say: Take our photo app's database server. On average it fails once every thousand hours, about every six weeks.
Version one, manual recovery. Nobody notices for thirty minutes, until users complain. That's the detection time.
Then an engineer logs in, diagnoses, and promotes the replica: another thirty minutes. So M-T-T-R is about an hour.
Availability: a thousand over a thousand and one, about ninety-nine point nine percent.
Version two, same failure rate. A health check spots it and automatic failover finishes in ten seconds.

Availability: about ninety-nine point nine nine nine seven percent. Three nines to five, without the machine failing any less. At scale something is always failing, so cutting M-T-T-R is usually the cheaper lever.

head: Property
Question
Measure
rows: Can I use it right now?
Chance of losing an object per year

steps.say: Three words people mix up. Availability: can I use it right now?
Reliability: does it do the right thing over time? A system can be available but unreliable, answering fast with wrong data.
Durability: will saved data survive crashes and dead disks? A system can be down but durable: offline for an hour, nothing lost.
Think of a bank. The cash machine works when you walk up: availability.
It gives the right amount and debits the right account: reliability.
Your balance survives a flood at the branch: durability.

A real number: S-three is designed for eleven nines of durability. Store ten million objects and you'd lose one about once in ten thousand years. But availability is only four nines. Separate promises, separate techniques: availability from redundancy and failover, durability from copies in separate places, writing to disk before confirming, and backups.
And replication isn't backup. A bug that deletes your photos is faithfully copied to every replica. Only a backup brings them back.
Pause: can a system be durable but not available? Yes. A database down for maintenance can't be read, but its data is safe on disk. Recap: usable now, correct over time, data survives.

A fault is one part going wrong. A failure is the whole system not serving users. Fault tolerance stops faults becoming failures, like a twin-engine plane landing on one engine. Here are five kinds of fault, each in our photo app. Hardware: a disk in the database server dies. Defence: a replica on another machine.
Software: a release leaks memory and app servers crash every few hours. Defence: tests, and rolling out to five percent first.
Network: a link between two zones drops packets. Defence: timeouts, retries, and replicas in other zones.
Human: someone pushes a config pointing every server at the wrong database. Defence: reviews, backups, and fast rollback. Big cloud outages are often this kind.
Dependency: the third-party face-tagging A-P-I is slow. Defence: timeouts, a fallback that skips tagging, and a circuit breaker that stops calling it for a while.

scenes.title: Failure models: how a broken part behaves

steps.say: Faults also differ by how the broken part behaves. These are failure models. Each row allows more misbehaviour than the last, so it's harder to tolerate. Here's a real case for each.
Fail-stop: the part halts, and everyone is reliably told. It's an idealisation, approximated by fencing: a power switch cuts a suspect node off, so the rest know for sure it's down.

Crash-stop: the process halts silently, say killed by the operating system for using too much memory. Nobody is told, and a dead node looks exactly like a slow one. Majority quorums need two f plus one nodes to survive f crashes: three survive one.

Crash-recovery: the node crashes and restarts with only what it saved to disk. A server loses power, reboots, and replays its write-ahead log. Anything it acknowledged but held only in memory is gone, so write durably before you acknowledge.

Omission: the node keeps running but drops some messages. A full network buffer silently loses a payment-done message. The sender retries, so the handler must be idempotent, or the customer pays twice.

Timing: right answers, too late. A database node freezes for ten seconds in a garbage-collection pause. Its leader lease expires, another node takes over, and the old one wakes up still thinking it leads. Defences: timeouts, deadlines, careful leases.

Byzantine: anything at all, even lies. In twenty oh eight, an Amazon S-three outage of several hours was traced to a single flipped bit in the servers' internal status messages. Defences are checksums and signatures, and full Byzantine tolerance needs three f plus one replicas. That's why Raft survives one crash with three nodes, but a Byzantine protocol needs four.

Most data centres assume crash-recovery, omission and timing faults, and add checksums for corrupted data. Then you handle a fault in three moves. Say the thumbnail service starts hanging. Detect: a health check every five seconds fails three times in a row.
Isolate: app servers call it with a two-second timeout. Without that, a dependency taking thirty seconds to fail ties up every thread, and the whole app hangs. A fast error is better than a slow one.
Recover: route around the bad copies and restart them. Uploads still work. Thumbnails are just late.

And watch for correlated failure: one bad deploy breaks every copy at once. Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly kills production servers so teams have to build for this. Recap: faults happen to parts, failures to the system.

scenes.title: Redundancy, SPOFs and failover
bullets: Ask of every box: if it vanishes?

steps.say: Redundancy means a spare for each critical part.
A single point of failure, a spof, is any part whose loss alone stops everything: one database, one load balancer, one D-N-S provider, even one engineer who knows the password.
Failover moves work to the spare, like a hospital switching to backup generators within seconds of a blackout.
To find spofs, ask of every box: if this disappears, what happens? Let's do that to the photo app.

scenes.title: Hunting SPOFs in the photo app

steps.say: D-N-S. If our one D-N-S provider goes down, nobody can find the app at all. Fix: a second provider, or a managed service that's redundant inside.
Load balancer. A single one is a spof. Run a pair, or use a managed one.
App servers. We run three across zones. Lose one and the others carry on. Not a spof.
Database. One primary. If it dies, every upload and every cache miss fails. That's our biggest spof. Fix: a standby in another zone with automatic failover.
Cache. If it dies, nothing is lost, but all fifteen thousand peak reads hit the database at once and swamp it. So run cache replicas too.
Object storage. A managed service that already copies data across zones. Fine. Common mistake: making app servers redundant but leaving one database, or putting all the copies in one rack.

scenes.title: Active-passive versus active-active
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  subgraph AP["Active-passive"]
    C1["Clients"] --> P["Primary serves all"]
    P -.->|"replicates"| S["Standby idle"]
  end
  subgraph AA["Active-active"]
    C2["Clients"] --> LB["Load balancer"]
    LB --> N1["Node 1 serves"]
    LB --> N2["Node 2 serves"]
  end
scenes.caption: Passive for single-writer databases, active for stateless

steps.say: Two ways to run the copies. Active-passive: a primary serves everything and replicates to an idle standby. Simple, but failover takes seconds to minutes. It suits single-writer databases, like our photo database.

Active-active: all nodes serve, and survivors absorb a failure. Better use of hardware and faster recovery, but hard for databases, where two writers can conflict. It suits stateless services, like our app servers.
Standbys come in three temperatures. Let's apply each to the photo database dying at eight p.m.
Cold standby: the spare is only last night's backup. Someone restores it onto a fresh machine. That takes hours, and every photo since the backup is lost. Cheap, and fine for an internal tool.
Warm standby: a replica is already running, but copying a few minutes behind. Promote it and you're back in minutes, maybe losing the last few seconds of writes.

Hot standby: a replica fully in sync, confirming every write before the primary acknowledges it. Failover is automatic, in seconds, losing nothing. A real managed example: Amazon R-D-S Multi-A-Z keeps a synchronous standby in another zone and fails over on its own, typically within a minute or two.
How many spares? If N servers handle peak, run N plus one to survive a failure: if thirteen handle peak, run fourteen. N plus two, fifteen, survives a failure during maintenance.
Two warnings. Split brain: if a slow primary is wrongly declared dead, two primaries accept writes and the data forks. And test failover, because untested failover fails when you need it.

scenes.title: Scalability
bullets: Name the parameter and the factor
Geography: Sydney as fast as Virginia

steps.say: Scalability is handling more load by adding resources, without a redesign and without collapsing. A restaurant that serves more diners by adding tables and cooks scales. One whose tiny kitchen tops out at fifty meals an hour doesn't.
Always name the load parameter and the factor. Not, it's scalable. Say: we can go to ten times the requests per second by adding servers.
Four dimensions, shown on the photo app. Load: peak reads grow from fifteen thousand to a hundred and fifty thousand a second.
Data: one terabyte a day becomes nearly two petabytes in five years.
Geography: users in Sydney want the feed as fast as users in Virginia.

Organisation: the team grows from five engineers to fifty, who must ship without stepping on each other. Techniques: stateless servers, caches, replicas, sharding, queues and C-D-Ns. Scale the real bottleneck, and make the next ten times easy, not a thousand.

scenes.title: Vertical and horizontal scaling
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  subgraph V["Vertical: scale up"]
    S1["4 cores, 16 GB"] -->|"upgrade"| S2["64 cores, 512 GB"]
  end
  subgraph H["Horizontal: scale out"]
    LB["Load balancer"] --> M1["Server"]
    LB --> M2["Server"]
    LB --> M3["Server"]
  end
scenes.caption: Bigger bus, or more buses

steps.say: Vertical scaling, scaling up, makes one machine bigger: a bigger bus. Horizontal scaling, scaling out, adds machines: more buses.
Scaling up is often just a config change in the cloud. Scaling out needs work you can divide. Stateless app servers are easy. Database writes need sharding: each machine holds part of the data.

scenes.title: Scaling the photo app as it grows

steps.say: Let's grow the photo app. At launch, a thousand users: one machine with four cores and sixteen gigabytes runs everything. That's correct, not lazy.
At a hundred thousand users, it's busy. Scale up: stop it, pick a sixty-four core, five hundred gigabyte machine, start it. A few minutes of downtime, zero code changes.
At a million users, one machine is a spof. Scale out the app tier: three stateless servers behind a load balancer. Keep one big database, plus a standby.
At ten million users, the database is the limit. Send reads to replicas and a cache. That's out for reads, but writes still go to one primary.
Beyond that, writes outgrow the biggest machine. Now shard: split users across several databases. That's real redesign work, so you delay it.
Up is simple, with no code change.
But it has a hard ceiling: the biggest machine you can buy.
And it's still a spof, with big boxes costing disproportionately more.
Out is practically unlimited.
Losing a node loses only a fraction, and you add nodes live.
But it needs statelessness or sharding, and consistency gets harder. Don't dismiss scaling up: Stack Overflow in twenty sixteen ran a huge site on eleven web servers and four database servers.

scenes.title: Elasticity
bullets: Above 70% CPU for 5 min: add; below 30%: remove

steps.say: Elasticity is scaling up and down automatically as load changes, so you pay for roughly what you use. Scalability says we can grow. Elasticity says we grow and shrink by ourselves, like a supermarket opening checkouts when queues get long.
Autoscaling watches a metric, like C-P-U, requests per second or queue length. Above a threshold, add servers. Below another, remove some. Serverless platforms can even scale to zero.
The limits: containers start in seconds, virtual machines in minutes, so a sudden spike can outrun you. Mostly stateless parts are elastic. And over-eager scale-down causes flapping.

scenes.title: Black Friday for an online shop

steps.say: An online shop normally runs ten app servers at about forty percent C-P-U.
At eight p.m. the Black Friday sale opens and traffic jumps four times in a few minutes. C-P-U passes seventy percent and stays there for five minutes, so the autoscaler adds servers.
Containers start in seconds, and the fleet grows to about thirty, with C-P-U near sixty percent. Virtual machines taking minutes would have left users with a slow first few minutes.
After midnight traffic falls and C-P-U drops below thirty percent. The autoscaler removes servers gradually, with a cooldown so it doesn't flap.
Next year they pre-scale at seven thirty on a schedule, so the spike never outruns them. In the interview: scalability is the capability, elasticity is doing it automatically, both ways.

scenes.title: Stateless and stateful services
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Stateful["Stateful"]
    U1["User A"] --> SA["Server 1 holds the session"]
  end
  subgraph Stateless["Stateless"]
    U2["User A"] --> LB["Load balancer"]
    LB --> X1["Server 1"]
    LB --> X2["Server 2"]
    X1 --> R["Redis: sessions"]
    X2 --> R
  end
scenes.caption: Sessions in Redis or a signed token, files in object storage

steps.say: State is data remembered between requests, like who's logged in, or a cart. A stateless service keeps none of it in its own memory, so any copy can serve any request, like a call centre where any agent can pull up your file. A stateful one ties you to one server, like a family doctor who keeps your history in their head: great until they're on holiday.
On the left, user A's session lives inside server one. On the right, any server can take the request, because the session lives in a shared Redis. Let's watch why that matters with one login.

scenes.title: One login session, step by step
bullets: 2. Next request hits server 2: logged out
3. Sticky sessions: fine until server 1 dies
4. Session in Redis, ID in a cookie
5. Or a signed token (JWT): no lookup
Any server can die; Redis needs spares too

steps.say: Step one. Priya logs in to the photo app. The load balancer sends her to server one, which stores her session in its own memory.
Step two. Her next tap goes to server two, which has never heard of her, so she's back at the login page. Local sessions plus a second server means random logouts. A classic bug.
Step three, the patch: sticky sessions. The load balancer always sends Priya to server one. It works, until server one crashes or gets redeployed, and every user on it is logged out at once.
Step four, the fix. Server one puts the session in Redis and gives Priya a cookie with just a session I-D. Any server looks it up in about half a millisecond.
Step five, the other fix: a signed token, a J-W-T, holding her user I-D. Any server checks the signature, with no lookup at all.

Now kill any server and Priya doesn't notice. The cost is that small extra hop, and Redis now needs its own spares, because the state moved, it didn't vanish. Game and chat servers stay stateful by nature, so they use sticky sessions and plan for that server dying.
Performance is speed for one request at the current load.
It's about latency and efficiency.
Diagnostic: send one request to an idle system. If even that's slow, it's performance.
Scalability is whether that speed holds as load grows.
Fast alone but slow under traffic: that's scalability.
A sports car is fast for one person but seats two. A train is slower off the mark but carries a thousand. Let's diagnose two real-looking complaints.

Complaint one: the feed takes two seconds even at three a.m., with almost no traffic. Even one request is slow, so it's performance. Profiling shows a query scanning all ten million photos because a column has no index. Add the index and it takes about five milliseconds. More servers would have done nothing.

Complaint two: the feed takes a hundred milliseconds alone, but three seconds at the evening peak. Fast alone, slow under load, so it's scalability. The database sits at a hundred percent, so add a cache and read replicas.
And one change can trade them: a hop to a shared cache costs every request half a millisecond, but lets you scale out. Recap: diagnose which one before you fix.
Concurrency is many tasks in progress over the same period, interleaved while each one waits.
It's about how work is organised, and one core is enough.
Rob Pike, a co-creator of Go, put it this way: concurrency is dealing with lots of things at once.
Parallelism is tasks running at the very same instant.
It's about execution, and needs multiple cores or machines.
Parallelism is doing lots of things at once. Let's see both in a kitchen, then in a web server.

scenes.title: A kitchen, then a web server

head: Setting
What happens
Kind
rows: Pasta boils while salad is chopped
Three dishes at the same moment
Overlaps the waits; 1 ms CPU each

steps.say: The kitchen. One cook puts pasta on to boil for ten minutes, and meanwhile chops the salad and plates a dessert. One person, three dishes in progress: concurrency.
Hire three cooks, each making a dish at the same moment. That's parallelism.

Now a web server. Each feed request spends fifty milliseconds waiting on the database and about one millisecond computing. One blocking thread handles one request at a time: one divided by point zero five is twenty requests a second, mostly waiting.

An event loop sends query A, doesn't wait, starts request B, and finishes each when its result arrives. The same thread now handles roughly a thousand a second, limited only by that millisecond of C-P-U. That's how Node and NGINX work. Threads and goroutines are other routes to concurrency.
Parallelism is for C-P-U-heavy work. Resizing a hundred photos at two hundred milliseconds each takes twenty seconds on one core, and about two and a half seconds across eight.
But Amdahl's law caps it. If ten percent of a job must run serially, even infinite cores give at most ten times.

scenes.title: Concurrency hazards
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Request A reads balance 100"] --> C["A writes 90"]
  B["Request B reads balance 100"] --> D["B writes 90"]
  C --> E["Final balance 90, not 80"]
  D --> E
scenes.caption: A race condition: one withdrawal is lost

steps.say: Shared data brings hazards. A race condition: two withdrawals of ten both read a balance of a hundred, both write ninety, and one withdrawal vanishes.
Deadlock: task one holds lock A and waits for B, task two holds B and waits for A, forever. Locks, atomic operations and transactions handle these.

Rules: use concurrency for I-O-bound work that mostly waits. Use parallelism for C-P-U-bound work, with no more C-P-U threads than cores. Interview question: is single-threaded Node concurrent? Yes, through its event loop. But not parallel for JavaScript, so run several processes for more cores.

head: Resource
Signs
Usual fixes
rows: High disk wait, IOPS at limit

steps.say: A bottleneck is the part that limits capacity, like a bottle's narrow neck. Fixing anything else won't help. Each of the four resources has its own symptom. C-P-U: near a hundred percent, latency rising with load.
Memory: swapping to disk, out-of-memory crashes, or a cache whose hit rate falls.
Disk: high wait times, with I-O-P-S or megabytes per second at their limit.
Network: a saturated link and dropped packets.

scenes.title: Four bottlenecks in the photo app

head: Resource
Symptom in the photo app
Fix
rows: 80 GB hot set, 64 GB cache: 95% to 70%

steps.say: C-P-U. Someone made app servers resize photos inside the upload request. C-P-U pins at a hundred percent and uploads take four seconds. Fix: move resizing to workers on the queue.

Memory. The cache box has sixty-four gigabytes, but the hot set has grown to eighty. The hit rate falls from ninety-five to seventy percent, so misses go from five to thirty percent. That's six times the database load. Fix: more cache memory or more nodes.

Disk. The database's cloud disk allows three thousand I-O-P-S, but cache misses now need five thousand random reads a second. Disk wait climbs, and p ninety-nine with it, while C-P-U looks idle. Fix: buy more I-O-P-S, move to N-V-M-e, or fix the cache first.
Network. Twenty gigabits a second of photos through ten gigabit cards. Links saturate and packets drop. Fix: a C-D-N.

Disks have two separate limits. I-O-P-S counts small random operations per second, like lookups. Throughput counts megabytes per second for big sequential transfers. A hard disk does about seventy-five to a hundred and fifty I-O-P-S, because the arm must move.
A SATA S-S-D: tens of thousands, at about five hundred megabytes a second.
N-V-M-e: hundreds of thousands to about a million.

A cloud g-p-three disk starts at three thousand I-O-P-S and a hundred and twenty-five megabytes per second. So twenty thousand random reads a second needs over a hundred hard disks, or one N-V-M-e drive.

scenes.title: Finding the bottleneck
bullets: 2. Find the limit or the growing queue
Find the queue: disk, pool, lock, network

steps.say: Step one, measure each resource under load. Don't guess.
Step two, look for the one at its limit, or a queue growing in front of something: a full thread pool, exhausted database connections, lock waits. Also hot rows and rate limits.
Step three, fix it and measure again. The bottleneck moves. Fix the cache and the network may be next.
Pause: latency rises under load, but C-P-U is at thirty percent. Where do you look?
Elsewhere: disk, network, a pool, a lock, a slow dependency. Find where requests queue. Most web services are I-O bound.

scenes.title: How to approach a system design interview
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  R["1. Requirements 5 min"] --> E["2. Estimates 3-5 min"]
  E --> A["3. API 5 min"]
  A --> D["4. Data model 5 min"]
  D --> H["5. High-level design 10 min"]
  H --> DD["6. Deep dives 10-15 min"]
  DD --> T["7. Trade-offs 3-5 min"]
scenes.caption: Seven steps for a 45-minute interview

steps.say: Last concept: the interview itself. Forty-five to sixty open-ended minutes. A repeatable seven-step structure shows how you think.

Requirements, five minutes. Estimates, three to five. A-P-I, five. Data model, five. High-level design, ten. Deep dives, ten to fifteen. Trade-offs and wrap-up, three to five. Let's run all seven on a classic question: design a U-R-L shortener.

scenes.title: Seven steps on a URL shortener

head: Step
URL shortener
rows: Stale cache, DB SPOF, shard at 10x

steps.say: Step one, requirements. Never start by drawing. Functional, what it does: shorten a long link, redirect, expire after a year. Non-functional, how well: a hundred million new links a month, redirects under fifty milliseconds at p ninety-nine, four nines, never lose a link. Out of scope: analytics and accounts.

Step two, estimates. A month is about two point six million seconds, so a hundred million links is about forty writes a second. At a hundred reads per write: four thousand redirects a second, twelve thousand at peak. At five hundred bytes a link, that's six hundred gigabytes a year. One database fits, and a hundred to one reads means caching matters.
Step three, the A-P-I. POST slash links with the long U-R-L returns a short code. GET slash code returns a three oh one redirect to the long U-R-L.
Step four, the data model. One links table: short code as the primary key, long U-R-L, expiry. Every read is a lookup by key.

Step five, the high-level design: load balancer, stateless app servers, cache, database. Walk one write: make a code, insert the row, return it. Walk one read: check the cache, on a miss read the database, then redirect.

Step six, deep dives. Codes without collisions: seven characters from sixty-two letters and digits gives about three and a half trillion codes, from a counter or random with a uniqueness check. And a celebrity's viral link stays in the cache, so it never hammers the database.

Step seven, trade-offs and wrap-up. The cache can serve a deleted link for a minute. The single database primary is a spof, so add a hot standby. At ten times the load, shard by short code. Then check the design against the requirements you wrote down.

head: Requirement
Measure
Main levers
rows: Who sees a write, how soon
Time to fix; cost per request

steps.say: Make each requirement measurable and name its lever. Availability: percent successful requests. Lever: redundancy and failover.
Latency: p ninety-nine per endpoint. Lever: caches, C-D-Ns, fewer trips.
Scalability: peak Q-P-S. Lever: stateless services, sharding, queues.
Consistency: after a write, who sees it, and how soon? For the shortener: a new link should work immediately. Lever: leaders, quorums, consensus.
Durability: never lose an acknowledged write. Lever: logs, replication, backups.
Reliability: error rate and M-T-T-R, via timeouts and retries. Security: authentication and encryption.

Maintainability means operable, simple and evolvable: dashboards per S-L-O, versioned schemas, canary deploys. And cost per request. Common mistakes: drawing before requirements, naming tech without reasons, and over-engineering a hundred Q-P-S system.

scenes.title: Episode 1 recap
bullets: Loop: goal, load, sketch, weak spots, fix
L = lambda x W; ns, 0.5 ms, 70-150 ms

steps.say: Design is a loop: goal, load, sketch, weak spots, fix. Built from eight standard boxes, each justified by a number.
Use percentiles, not averages, and fix the biggest latency term first. Latency explodes near full load.
Little's law sizes pools. RAM is nanoseconds, a data-centre trip half a millisecond, an ocean seventy to a hundred and fifty.
Divide per-day counts by ten to the five, then apply peak, utilisation and zone loss.
Three nines is forty-three minutes a month. One bad afternoon can spend it, so cut M-T-T-R and remove spofs.
Keep servers stateless, measure bottlenecks, and follow the seven steps. Next episode: networking, from D-N-S and T-C-P to load balancers.
